## Technical Corrections to This Historical Draft

This source is retained for audit history and is excluded from the production reading path. The corrections below govern its interpretation; the original wording is preserved separately.

Set $A(t)=D_x f(\bar x(t),\bar u(t))$ and $B(t)=D_u f(\bar x(t),\bar u(t))$ along one differentiable nominal solution. With sufficient regularity to differentiate the flow, the displayed variation-of-constants formula is exact for first variations. Finite state/input differences additionally have nonlinear remainders.

The state-transition matrix is defined by $\partial_t\Phi(t,s)=A(t)\Phi(t,s)$ and $\Phi(s,s)=I$. It transports a derivative through the linearized dynamics; it is not a curvature tensor or a measure of the nominal curve's bending. Time-varying coefficients can amplify variations even when instantaneous eigenvalues suggest decay. The placeholder figure below is historical, not missing evidence for a new claim. See [canonical dynamics](../../../tangent-hyperplanes-series/part-2-dynamics.html).

## 1. Variational Equations

For a nonlinear system,

$$
\dot{x} = f(x,u),
$$

variations satisfy

$$
\delta \dot{x} = A(t)\delta x + B(t)\delta u.
$$

This equation governs the exact evolution of infinitesimal perturbations.

## 2. State Transition Operator

The solution is

$$
\delta x(t_1)
= \Phi(t_1,t_0)\delta x(t_0)
+ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \Phi(t_1,t)B(t)\delta u(t)\,dt.
$$

All integrated effects are linearly accumulated *after transport*.
